title: A scoping review on how generative artificial intelligence transforms assessment in higher education
authors: Qi Xia; Xiaojing Weng; Fan Ouyang; Tzung‐Jin Lin; Thomas K. F. Chiu
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
source_used: Publisher OA PDF (Springer, CC BY 4.0) via https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1186/s41239-024-00468-z.pdf; saved as pdfs/R03.pdf
ft_reason: HE context; assessment transformation and academic integrity under GenAI is the primary focus; peer-reviewed scoping review (2024, English).
study_design: Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) of empirical studies; ERIC, Web of Science, Scopus; search completed 30 Sep 2023
country: Hong Kong/China and Taiwan (authors); reviewed studies from 18 regions
discipline: Multi-disciplinary (education, medicine and computer science most common among 11 disciplines)

key_findings.finding: Of the 27 articles addressing students, 54% flagged GenAI as a significant challenge to academic integrity, with evidence that ChatGPT can pass exams and achieve high grades on short-form essays.

Reviewed studies called for more diverse and innovative assessment; presentations and live or pre-recorded discussions were rated least affected by ChatGPT, and video-conference questioning was proposed as an alternative.
key_findings.location: pp. 8-9, Sec 'More diverse and innovative assessment'

key_findings.finding: Short-term mitigations reported in the literature include oral presentations, in-person exams, projects and laboratory work, since face-to-face knowledge-based assessment was seen as not threatened by ChatGPT.
At teacher level, the review identifies needs for assessment and AI literacy and a balanced, mixed human/AI assessment approach in which teachers assess ideas and reasoning that GenAI cannot.
key_findings.location: pp. 7-10, Fig. 4; Sec 'Balancing GenAI and human assessment'

key_findings.finding: At institution level, assessment policies need redesign, including clear GenAI usage rules; transparent disclosure of tool use may mean use is not treated as plagiarism.

dimensions.authenticity: Reports calls for authentic, higher-order and case-based tasks that are hard for AI to replicate (pp. 9-10).
dimensions.capability_verification: Reports that ChatGPT passes many exams and essays, undermining traditional tasks as evidence of student learning (p. 7, p. 13).
dimensions.integrity_security: Integrity is the main student-level challenge (54% of articles); in-person and oral formats are proposed as more secure (pp. 7, 13).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Argues critical thinking, problem solving, creativity and AI/digital literacy should be explicit learning outcomes and assessed (p. 9, p. 14).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Recommends balancing AI-assisted and human assessment and clear institutional rules on GenAI use (pp. 10-11).
dimensions.workload: Notes assessment was historically manual and time-intensive and that GenAI may provide immediate feedback (pp. 2, 5-6); no workload data.
dimensions.feasibility: Calls for teacher professional development in assessment and AI literacy as a precondition for change (p. 14).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Notes possible bias in GenAI feedback and the need for equitable AI access (pp. 2, 6).

author_recommendations: Provide teacher professional development on assessment, AI and digital literacy (not tested).
Strengthen teacher beliefs about combining human and AI assessment, moving to mixed methods (not tested).
Institutions should review assessment policies, diversify assessment beyond exams and essays, and offer more interdisciplinary programmes (not tested).
Future research on discipline-tailored assessment strategies and standardised assessment policy (not tested).
limitations: Authors note that, as a scoping review, it cannot give specific recommendations and that many included studies discussed GenAI generically without naming technologies (p. 17). Most included studies date from 2023; there was a single search date (30 Sep 2023) and no quality appraisal of the included studies is reported.

quality.note: Clear RQs, PRISMA-ScR process with dual coding and a coding table; limitations stated briefly. Synthesis is descriptive and percentages are based on small counts.

title: The Artificial Intelligence Assessment Scale (AIAS): A Framework for Ethical Integration of Generative AI in Educational Assessment
authors: Mike Perkins; Leon Furze; Jasper Roe; Jason Alexander MacVaugh
venue: Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice
source_used: Publisher OA PDF (JUTLP) via https://open-publishing.org/journals/index.php/jutlp/article/download/810/769; saved as pdfs/R10.pdf
ft_reason: Formal framework paper for GenAI in HE assessment and integrity, peer-reviewed journal (2024, English).
study_design: Conceptual framework paper (AI Assessment Scale) grounded in a literature review
discipline: Discipline-agnostic (HE generally; notes it is applicable to K-12)
sample: Not applicable (no empirical data; the scale had only been piloted in one cohort, with no reported results)
genai_tools: GenAI generally (ChatGPT, GPT-4, image generation tools)

key_findings.finding: Proposes a five-level AI Assessment Scale (No AI; AI-assisted idea generation and structuring; AI-assisted editing; AI task completion with human evaluation; Full AI) so educators can set permitted GenAI use per task based on learning outcomes.

Recommends that Level 1 (No AI) tasks be supervised or low-stakes formative, because unsupervised no-AI conditions raise equity concerns and AI use may be undetectable; examples include viva voce and technology-free oral discussion.
At Level 3, students submit their original work alongside the AI-edited version, and at Level 4 any AI-created content must be cited; Level 3 is framed as a transitional stop-gap.
Argues that treating AI-generated text as inherently misconduct is unsustainable, that detection approaches are flawed, and that misuse is better handled through rubrics than as integrity breaches.
Highlights unequal access to paid or advanced GenAI tools as an equity issue and suggests standardising which tools are permitted.
key_findings.location: pp. 11-12, Sec 'Balancing Skill Development, Engagement, and Ethics'

dimensions.authenticity: Higher levels (L4-L5) are linked to authentic and industry-style tasks that reflect professional AI use (pp. 5, 10).
dimensions.capability_verification: Level 1 under supervision, including viva voce, is the route to verify unaided knowledge and skills (p. 8).
dimensions.integrity_security: Acknowledges the scale does not stop students disguising AI use and that detection tools are flawed (pp. 4, 12).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Educators choose the AIAS level according to the learning outcomes being addressed (abstract; p. 12).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: The core contribution: graded, cumulative levels that tell students where GenAI use is permitted (pp. 6-10).
dimensions.scalability: Presented as simple and quick to implement at institutional level and adaptable to local policy (pp. 1, 7).
dimensions.feasibility: Recommends supporting guidelines and multimedia material and notes the scale must be continually updated as tools evolve (pp. 8, 12).
dimensions.process_visibility: Level 3 requires the original work in an appendix and Level 4 requires citing AI content, which makes the process partly visible (pp. 7, 9-10).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Unequal access to premium tools and to language fluency is a key concern; suggests standardising permitted tools (pp. 8, 11-13).

author_recommendations: Adopt the five-level AIAS and tailor it to institutional policy (not tested).
Run Level 1 (No AI) tasks under supervision or as low-stakes formative tasks (not tested).
Develop student-facing guidelines on ethics, citation and limitations of GenAI (not tested).
Handle GenAI misuse through assessment rubrics rather than as an academic integrity breach (not tested).
Conduct empirical studies of the AIAS in diverse settings (not tested).
limitations: Authors state there is no empirical evidence of the scale's effectiveness (only a recent pilot), that it may not suit all assessments and must be adapted to learning outcomes, that it cannot stop students disguising GenAI use, and that it needs ongoing updating as the technology changes (p. 12).

quality.note: Clear aim and argument grounded in cited literature; no data, so q3 is N and q4 is Unclear (claims of effectiveness not evaluated); limitations explicitly stated.

title: Beyond Detection: Redesigning Authentic Assessment in an AI-Mediated World
authors: Steven Kickbusch; Kevin Ashford-Rowe; Andrew Kemp; Jennifer Boreland; Henk Huijser
source_used: MDPI OA PDF and HTML both returned HTTP 403 (access denied to automated retrieval); OpenAlex/Unpaywall list no other copy. Abstract taken from OpenAlex.
ft_reason: From abstract: HE assessment redesign for authenticity and integrity with GenAI; peer-reviewed journal (2025, English). Full text is gold OA but could not be retrieved automatically; recommend manual download for verification.
study_design: Conceptual paper with design patterns (per abstract)
discipline: Discipline-agnostic; examples from business and pre-service teacher education
genai_tools: ChatGPT, DALL-E, MS Copilot (named in abstract)

key_findings.finding: Argues surveillance and AI detection misdiagnose the problem; authenticity must be redesigned, not policed, in contexts where AI use is expected, declared and scrutinised.

Offers discipline-agnostic design patterns: students critique, adapt and verify AI outputs, provide process transparency (prompts, iterations, rationale) and demonstrate digital discernment and ethical judgement.
Proposes reflective artefacts such as metacognitive commentary, process logs and oral defences to make student thinking visible and reduce punitive approaches.

dimensions.authenticity: Reconceptualises authenticity as constructed in AI-present contexts that mirror professional knowledge work (abstract).
dimensions.capability_verification: Oral defences and reflective artefacts are proposed to make thinking visible and substantiate attribution (abstract).
dimensions.integrity_security: Positions integrity as anchored in design rather than detection (abstract).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: AI is positioned as a collaborator whose use is expected and declared (abstract).
dimensions.process_visibility: Process transparency through prompts, iterations, rationale and process logs is central (abstract).

author_recommendations: Design tasks requiring students to critique, adapt and verify AI outputs (not tested).
Require explicit process transparency (prompts, iterations, rationale) (not tested).
Use metacognitive commentary, process logs and oral defences (not tested).
limitations: Not reported in the abstract. Extraction is limited to the abstract; the paper is conceptual and its patterns appear not to have been evaluated.

quality.note: Extraction based on abstract/landing-page metadata only; no legal full text obtained, so no page locations. Conceptual paper with no data (q3 N).

title: Guidelines for learning design and assessment for generative artificial intelligence-integrated education: a unified view
authors: Andy Nguyen; Anh Duong; Diem Thi Nguyen; Van Thi Thanh Lai; Belle Dang
source_used: Publisher OA HTML full text (Emerald, CC BY 4.0) read via WebFetch at https://www.emerald.com/insight/content/doi/10.1108/ILS-11-2024-0148/full/html. PDF download was blocked by a bot challenge, so no PDF was saved. Locations given by section/table because no page numbers were available in the HTML.
ft_reason: Analyses intergovernmental (OECD, UNESCO, EU, Council of Europe) policy documents on GenAI in education generally. The paper does not frame its scope as higher education; the only explicit HE mention is a single citation in Sec 5. Fails IC1. Borderline: assessment and integrity are substantial, so flag for second-reviewer check.
study_design: Qualitative policy document analysis (thematic analysis, deductive and inductive)
sample: 8 IGO policy/guidance documents (Council of Europe x2, European Commission, OECD x2, UNESCO x3)

key_findings.finding: Policy documents agree on higher-order thinking (critical thinking, problem solving, creativity) and AI evaluation literacy as outcomes; metacognition and self-regulated learning are underrepresented.

Under 'rethinking assessment objectives and means', documents stress higher-order thinking, cheat-proof tests (OECD1, UNESCO2) and formative assessment; authentic, personalised assessment is suggested as resilient. 'Cheat-proof' is not defined.
Only three documents address integrating AI into assignments and pedagogical practice, and guidance rarely explains how to design for transferable skills with AI.

Assessment design considerations cluster into four themes: GenAI-integrated pedagogical dimensions, accessibility and inclusiveness, holistic design, and ethical principles (data privacy has the strongest alignment).

dimensions.authenticity: Authentic assessment simulating real-world contexts is cited as a resilient design (Sec 3; Sec 4.2.1).
dimensions.integrity_security: Cheat-proof tests and integrity concerns appear in two documents but without operational detail (Sec 4.2.1, Table 2).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Synthesises the skills that policy documents want in learning outcomes (Sec 4.1, Table 1).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Advocates hybrid intelligence, where AI augments rather than replaces core cognition (Sec 5).
dimensions.feasibility: Calls for teacher professional development and supporting infrastructure (Sec 5, Table 4).
dimensions.process_visibility: Calls for assessment of both process and performance, using learner-generated evidence and reflection (Sec 3).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Equity of access, technical accessibility and the digital divide are recurring themes (Sec 4.3.2, 4.3.4).

author_recommendations: Adapt curricula and build GenAI literacy, with professional development for teachers (not tested).
Ensure equitable access, data privacy and transparency in policy (not tested).
Research how higher-order thinking can be authentically assessed with GenAI (not tested).
limitations: Authors state the analysis is limited to selected IGO documents and may miss regional or local nuances; future work should include developing-country documents and empirical testing of the guidelines (Sec 5).

quality.note: Clear RQs, documented sample and thematic process, tables trace each theme to its source documents, limitations stated. Read through a WebFetch rendering of the HTML rather than a saved PDF.

title: AI in action: Changes to student perceptions when using generative artificial intelligence for the creation of a multimedia project-based assessment
authors: Kellie A. Charles; Arsalan Yousuf; Han Chow Chua; Slade T. Matthews; Joanna Harnett; Tina Hinton
source_used: Elsevier (CC BY per OpenAlex) landing page and ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403; not in PMC/Europe PMC full text. Abstract taken from PubMed (PMID 40086582).
ft_reason: From abstract: HE capstone unit; piloted a GenAI-allowed authentic group multimedia assessment and studied AI use and integrity of the assessment process; peer-reviewed (2025, English). Recommend manual download of the OA version for verification.
study_design: Exploratory qualitative case study; thematic analysis of student logbooks using an AI role-based framework
sample: n = 40 students; 14 AI use cases across 5 groups
genai_tools: GenAI generally (specific tools not reported in abstract)

key_findings.finding: Before their projects, students saw AI mainly in a tutor-like role (Arbiter 49%, Oracle 41%, Quant 10%).
In practice AI use was limited to early-stage idea generation (Oracle, 86%) or data analysis (Quant, 14%), and no group used AI to write text for the final assessment.
The gap between perceived and actual use suggests student uncertainty when AI is permitted; the authors call for clear guidance on assessing the AI-supported learning process.

dimensions.authenticity: Piloted a collaborative group multimedia, project-based assessment intended to evaluate authentic learning (abstract).
dimensions.integrity_security: Authors argue clear guidance is needed to keep the assessment system's integrity when AI is allowed (abstract).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Students were uncertain about permitted AI use and used it less than expected (abstract).
dimensions.process_visibility: Logbooks documented the assessment process and AI use (abstract).

author_recommendations: Provide clear guidance for educators and students on how to assess the AI-supported learning process (not tested).
limitations: Not reported in the abstract. The abstract shows a small single-unit sample (n = 40), and this extraction is limited to the abstract.

quality.note: Extraction based on abstract/landing-page metadata only; no legal full text obtained, so no page locations. Abstract reports design and n, but not enough to judge sampling or analytic rigour.

title: Making sense of generative AI for assessments: Contrasting student claims and assessor evaluations
authors: Isabel Fischer; Simon Sweeney; Matthew Lucas; Neha Gupta
venue: The International Journal of Management Education
source_used: Warwick Research Archive (WRAP) PDF of the published CC BY version, https://wrap.warwick.ac.uk/id/eprint/188394/7/1-s2.0-S1472811724001526-main.pdf; saved as pdfs/R45.pdf
ft_reason: HE postgraduate assessment with GenAI use built in and AI-use reflection; compares student claims with assessor evaluation; peer-reviewed (2024, English).
study_design: Exploratory single case study (Yin); inductive qualitative content analysis with descriptive quantification of submissions
sample: 118 reflective essays from 118 postgraduate students, one module, May 2023
genai_tools: ChatGPT, Bard/Gemini, Grammarly, the school's AI Essay Analyst, DALL-E

key_findings.finding: The three-part authentic assessment (blog post, board briefing, 500-word AI-use reflection) required students to append the prompts and GenAI conversations they used.

Students' claims put 26.3% at sensemaking stage 1, 56.8% at stage 2 and 16.9% at stage 3; assessors placed 20.3%, 69.5% and 10.2% respectively, so only about one in ten showed critical evaluation of AI.

16 of 118 students claimed to have used a bespoke tool that no student had requested access to, some describing feedback it could not have given, which suggests that AI-use reflections can be fabricated.
Higher assessor-rated sensemaking stages went with modestly higher marks (+2.6% at stage 2 and +3.5% at stage 3 relative to stage 1).
Students most often named accuracy of results (32.2%) and lack of critical thinking (23.7%) as GenAI drawbacks; plagiarism (6.8%) and privacy (3.4%) were rarely raised.

dimensions.authenticity: Assessment designed to mirror real-world audiences (publishable blog, board briefing) (p. 3, Sec 2.1.1).
dimensions.capability_verification: Student self-reports of AI use did not match assessors' evaluation of demonstrated use (p. 8, Sec 3.3; Fig. 5).
dimensions.integrity_security: Fabricated claims of tool use show the limits of self-declaration as an integrity mechanism (p. 8).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Assessment criteria (comprehension, analysis, critical evaluation, writing) mapped to Bloom's and Driscoll's models (pp. 3-4, Fig. 3).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: School policy lets lecturers forbid, authorise or encourage GenAI; this module encouraged it (p. 2, p. 3).
dimensions.process_visibility: Prompts and conversations appended to submissions gave assessors evidence of the process (p. 3).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Notes concern about free versus paid GenAI access and disadvantage for students with weaker language skills (p. 9).

author_recommendations: Avoid or broaden lists of example tools in assignment briefs to reduce performative claims (not tested).
Use more directive brief language to encourage interpretive reflection (not tested).
Consider providing GenAI-generated model answers that students must exceed (not tested).
Develop programme-level synoptic assessments and test language proficiency independently (not tested).
Develop institutional AI strategies, AI literacy and staff professional development (not tested).
limitations: Authors note students may have written what they thought assessors wanted to hear, findings are context-specific (pre-experience Master's students, one UK business school, end-of-year timing with possible assessment fatigue) (p. 12, Sec 6). The single cross-sectional cohort limits replicability (p. 5, Sec 2.4).

quality.note: Clear aim, appropriate case design, sample and data collection described, findings tabulated, limitations stated. Coding reliability statistics are not reported.

key_findings.finding: Markers were generally unable to distinguish assessments with GenAI input from those without, although suspected GenAI presence changed how they marked.
The level of authenticity of an assessment had no effect on safeguarding against, or detecting, GenAI use.

Shift towards performative, synchronous interpersonal assessments that use social experiential learning (not tested).
Focus assessment on process and workplace relevance rather than output (not tested).

title: The rapid rise of generative AI and its implications for academic integrity: Students’ perceptions and use of chatbots for assistance with assessments
authors: Jan Henrik Gruenhagen; Peter M. Sinclair; Julie‐Anne Carroll; Philip Baker; Ann Wilson; Daniel Demant
source_used: UTS OPUS repository PDF (CC BY), http://hdl.handle.net/10453/179913; saved as pdfs/R57.pdf
ft_reason: HE students' use of GenAI chatbots for assessments and perceptions of academic integrity, with implications for assessment design; peer-reviewed (2024, English).
study_design: Cross-sectional online survey (correlational), with a supplementary thematic analysis of open-ended responses
discipline: Multi-disciplinary (includes Computer and Information Systems, Business, Health, Engineering and others)
sample: N = 337 Australian coursework students (April-June 2023); 78 gave qualitative comments

key_findings.finding: 79.5% had used a chatbot for some learning-related purpose, and 36.5% had used one for assistance with an assessment.

Of students reporting assessment use, 27.0% used chatbots to find information, 20.5% to analyse a topic, 17.8% to provide example writing for part or all of an assessment and 7.1% to solve a multiple-choice quiz.
Students gave low agreement that chatbot use is always an academic integrity breach (mean 3.6/10); students who had used chatbots for assessment agreed significantly less (2.5 vs 4.3).
Neither logistic regression model was significant overall; no psychosocial or demographic factor predicted chatbot use for assessments.
Only 33.5% had discussed chatbots with teachers versus 60.5% with peers; qualitative themes included levelling the playing field for neurodivergent and ESL students and concerns about over-reliance.

dimensions.authenticity: Argues GenAI is an opportunity to reimagine assessment as more authentic and less reliant on written knowledge recall (p. 8, Sec 5).
dimensions.integrity_security: Students commonly do not see chatbot use as cheating; authors warn a retreat to invigilated tasks may reduce authenticity (pp. 6, 8).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Recommends clear policies and co-designed codes of conduct on ethical GenAI use (p. 8, Sec 5-5.1).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Students reported chatbots supporting those with ADHD, autism, anxiety or ESL, while others raised fairness concerns about unequal access (pp. 6-7, Sec 4.5.1, 4.5.4).

author_recommendations: Define clear institutional policies and guidelines for ethical GenAI use in assessments (not tested).
Rethink assessment design towards authentic, real-world tasks rather than relying on invigilation (not tested).
Co-design codes of conduct with students and student unions, and run AI literacy campaigns (not tested).
Integrate critical evaluation of AI output and hands-on GenAI use into curricula (not tested).
limitations: Authors note a non-representative convenience sample with limited generalisability, Australia-only data, a cross-sectional design with no causal inference, and qualitative data limited to brief open-ended comments (p. 8, Sec 5.2).

quality.note: Clear RQs, validated scales with reported reliability, Bonferroni-adjusted analyses, limitations stated. Self-selected sample.

title: Beyond the ban: A theoretical framework for integrating Generative AI in assessment
source_used: SAGE (CC BY-NC) landing page and PDF returned HTTP 403 or a bot challenge; University of Canberra research profile lists no attached file. Abstract taken from OpenAlex.
ft_reason: From abstract: theoretical framework for GenAI in university assessment design, governance and integrity; peer-reviewed journal (2025, English). Recommend manual download of the OA version for verification.

key_findings.finding: Argues the core challenge is not cheating but misalignment between legacy assessment designs and AI-mediated learning, so universities must govern and design for GenAI rather than ban it.

Contributes a tiered governance model, an assessment redesign heuristic built on authenticity, cognitive demand and evidence provenance, and a Swiss-cheese risk-mitigation view centred on learning rather than surveillance.

Illustrates ready-to-adopt patterns: oral defence with an artefact trail, cohort-specific data briefs and constrained-tools practicals, plus governance levers such as template language and moderation workflows.

dimensions.capability_verification: Oral defence with an artefact trail and constrained-tools practicals are proposed to verify learning (abstract).
dimensions.integrity_security: Layered Swiss-cheese risk mitigation rather than surveillance (abstract).
dimensions.scalability: Claims a pathway that is feasible at scale through governance levers (abstract).
dimensions.feasibility: Specifies implementable levers: role clarity, template language, moderation workflows, analytics (abstract).
dimensions.process_visibility: Evidence provenance and artefact trails are central to the heuristic (abstract).

author_recommendations: Adopt a tiered governance model aligning policy, pedagogy and assessment operations (not tested).
Redesign assessments using the authenticity / cognitive demand / evidence provenance heuristic (not tested).
Use patterns such as oral defence with artefact trail, cohort-specific data briefs and constrained-tools practicals (not tested).
limitations: Not reported in the abstract; extraction limited to the abstract. The framework appears not to have been empirically evaluated.
